meta.title: Who really said "I'm so fast last night I cut the light switch and was in bed before the room was dark"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ali used the boast — but it was in print in 1917 and told about Cool Papa Bell in 1969, and his real 1974 wording differs from the line online.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'm so fast last night I cut the light switch and was in bed before the room was dark'?
meta.ogDescription: Ali said a version in 1974. But the light-switch boast dates to a 1917 Marines Magazine joke, and the wording online matches no transcript.

answer.label: Said by Ali — but not his line
answer.sourceLine: Ali really did use this boast — the Village Voice of 25 July 1974 printed it as “I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark,” and The New York Times printed another version in 1975. But he did not invent it: the same gag was in print in The Marines Magazine in April 1917, and the sentence circulating under his name matches neither wording any reporter actually transcribed.
answer.confidenceText: Ali used the boast, but it was a stock joke long before him — and this exact wording appears in no documented source.

source.heading: Where the joke actually starts

docMeta.dd: Village Voice, 25 July 1974, p. 9 — also The New York Times, 29 June 1975

source.excerpt: Corporal Smith is still in training and, believe me, he is some speed merchant. Here is one record he holds: It is 20 feet from the switchboard to his pile of alfalfa and he can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!
trail: April 1917 — the joke reaches print. A correspondent writing as “Hablarias” in The Marines Magazine credits a Corporal Smith at Fort Mifflin, Pennsylvania, who “can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!” That is a quarter-century before Ali was born — Quote Investigator ↗.

1919–1945 — a stage gag. The Chicago Tribune found the vaudeville team Moran and Mack using it in 1919, a Kansas paper gave it to an Atchison husband and a gas lamp in 1920, and a published Abbott and Costello radio script was still working it in 1945 — Quote Investigator ↗.

1969 — it becomes a baseball legend. Satchel Paige attached it to James “Cool Papa” Bell, and Bell later explained at a 1981 Negro Baseball Reunion that a room light with a roughly three-second delay let him make the tall tale look true — Society for American Baseball Research ↗.

1974 — Ali’s turn. Nick Browne recorded him for the Village Voice of 25 July 1974: “I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark.” Robert Lipsyte printed another version in The New York Times on 29 June 1975 — Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The oldest known form of the boast, printed a quarter-century before Ali was born. For comparison, Ali’s own documented wording, recorded by the Village Voice on 25 July 1974: “I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark.”

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording on this page, because that wording cannot be tied to any published source. The joke’s earliest documented appearance — The Marines Magazine, April 1917 — is old enough to be public domain in the United States, but Ali’s own documented versions were printed in the Village Voice in 1974 and The New York Times in 1975, and those articles remain in copyright.

author.name: Muhammad Ali
author.heading: About Muhammad Ali
author.bio: Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky on 17 January 1942, Ali held the heavyweight title across three separate reigns and became one of the most quoted athletes who ever lived. His public voice was as much a performance as his boxing: he released two Grammy-nominated spoken-word albums and is often named as a forerunner of hip-hop for his freestyle rhyming and braggadocio. That gift was partly collection — Ali picked up stock boasts, sharpened them and delivered them better than anyone else, which is exactly what happened with the light-switch line. He died on 3 June 2016.

copyAttribution: Not originally Muhammad Ali's. The boast — turning off the light and being in bed before the room goes dark — was in print by April 1917 in The Marines Magazine, was used by the vaudeville team Moran and Mack in 1919 and by Abbott and Costello in a 1945 radio script, and was applied by Satchel Paige to Cool Papa Bell in 1969. Ali's own documented version, recorded by the Village Voice on 25 July 1974: "I'm so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark." Source: Quote Investigator, "Quote Origin: When He Turned Out the Light He Was in Bed Before the Room Was Dark," 12 June 2013.

misattribution.heading: Who the joke really belongs to
misattribution.intro: The line is genuinely Ali-adjacent — he told versions of it to reporters in 1974 and 1975. What is not genuine is the idea that he invented it, or that the sentence circulating under his name is something he was ever recorded saying.

items.who: An anonymous Marine Corps correspondent, April 1917
items.why: Writing as “Hablarias” from Fort Mifflin, Pennsylvania, he reported that Corporal Smith “can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!” This is the oldest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Moran and Mack (1919); Abbott and Costello (1945)
items.why: The Chicago Tribune caught the comedy team Moran and Mack running it as a two-hander: “Am I quick? Why, man, when I go to bed at night and turn out the light I’m in bed before the room is dark.” A published Abbott and Costello radio script was still using it in 1945 — Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Satchel Paige, about James “Cool Papa” Bell
items.why: Paige’s tribute to the Negro Leagues outfielder is where most people first met the joke. The National Baseball Hall of Fame still prints it — “Cool Papa was so fast he could flip the light switch and be in bed before the room got dark” — and notes it may have had literal truth, because a room they shared had a faulty switch connection: Baseball Hall of Fame ↗.

The circulating sentence — and the even smoother “turned off the light switch in my hotel room” variant found on quote-aggregator sites — matches neither version a reporter took down. Wikiquote’s Ali page carries no form of the line at all: Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Ali took a boast that had been in print since 1917 and made it his own. The words he was actually recorded using, in the Village Voice of 25 July 1974, were “I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark” — Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the joke keeps finding a new owner
lead: This is a folk joke that attaches itself to whoever is currently the fastest person alive. In 1917 it belonged to a Corporal Smith at Fort Mifflin; by 1919 it was a two-hander on the vaudeville stage; in 1920 a Kansas paper gave it to an Atchison woman’s husband and a gas lamp; in 1937 it went to the child Paul Bunyan and a candle; in 1945 Lou Costello was doing it on the radio. Then Satchel Paige pinned it on Cool Papa Bell, and it became a baseball legend rather than a gag.

By the time Ali reached for it in the mid-1970s he was doing what he always did with inherited material — taking a line the audience half-recognised and making it sound like it had been invented on the spot. That is a real skill, and it is not the same thing as authorship. The reason the quote sits under his name today is simply that he was the last and loudest person to tell it.
detailsBody: 1917 — Corporal Smith, Fort Mifflin, Pennsylvania, in The Marines Magazine.
1919 — the comedy team Moran and Mack, on the vaudeville circuit, reported in the Chicago Tribune.
1920 — an Atchison, Kansas husband, with a gas light instead of a switch.
1937 — Paul Bunyan as a boy, blowing out a candle.
1943 — a Washington Post brainteaser, whose answer was “simply go to bed in the daytime.”
1945 — Abbott and Costello, in a published radio script.
1969 and 1971 — Satchel Paige, about James “Cool Papa” Bell.
1973 — the San Diego Padres shortstop Enzo Hernández, in the Washington Post.
1974 and 1975 — Muhammad Ali, in the Village Voice and The New York Times.
context.pull: In print since 1917 — a quarter-century before Ali was born.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the boast to April 1917 in The Marines Magazine (correspondent "Hablarias", Fort Mifflin PA, p. 32: "he can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!"), then Moran and Mack in the Chicago Tribune 1919, an Atchison/Kansas gas-light version 1920, Paul Bunyan 1937, a Washington Post brainteaser 1943, an Abbott and Costello script 1945, Satchel Paige on Cool Papa Bell 1969 (Washington Post) and 1971 (Jet), Enzo Hernandez 1973, and Muhammad Ali in the Village Voice 25 July 1974 ("I'm so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark") and the New York Times 29 June 1975. QI concludes the joke was in circulation by 1917 and was adopted by many comedians and athletes.

SABR's "How Fast Was Cool Papa Bell?" reports Paige's claim that Bell "was so fast that he could turn out the light and jump in bed before it got dark," and gives Bell's own 1981 Negro Baseball Reunion explanation that a light switch had a delay of about three seconds, which he used to trick Paige. The article does not mention Muhammad Ali.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame's Cool Papa Bell page (life dates 1903-1991, inducted 1974) carries Paige's line "Cool Papa was so fast he could flip the light switch and be in bed before the room got dark," and notes the story may have had literal truth because a room they shared had a faulty switch connection.
Wikiquote's Muhammad Ali page contains no version of the light-switch boast in any section (not in Quotes, Misattributed, or Quotes about Ali).

Wikipedia confirms Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. on 17 January 1942 in Louisville, Kentucky, died 3 June 2016 in Scottsdale, Arizona, held heavyweight titles including the undisputed championship 1974-1978, and was known for boasts, poetry and two Grammy-nominated spoken-word albums.
